Medications
Due to the complex nature of PN solutions most medications should not be added as there is 
potential for instability and incompatibility. However, some medications such as histamine H2 
receptor agonists, are used to decrease gastric secretions. Regular short-acting insulin can be added 
to the PN solution to control blood sugars. Other medications, such as octreotide, heparin, corti­
costeroids and metoclopramide can be added to the PN solution when needed.

Part IV  Fundamentals of Oncology and Nutrition Support
Monitoring and Management of Complications
Non-Infectious Catheter Complications
Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT) is a severe immune-mediated adverse reaction that 
occurs by intravascular platelet aggregation that can develop into arterial and venous thrombus. 
Catheter occlusions can also occur and are classified as either a complete or incomplete occlusion. 
In a complete occlusion, fluid cannot be instilled and blood cannot be aspirated out, whereas an 
incomplete occlusion, fluid can be infused yet blood cannot be aspirated. A venous thrombus can 
occur if the catheter tip is malpostitioned and can be diagnosed via duplex ultrasound or venogram. 
A tunneled catheter breakage must be repaired urgently to prevent air embolism, leakage of blood, 
and bacterial contamination. An air embolism is a rare yet potentially fatal complication where 
either during or after insertion, there is catheter breakage or a disconnection of caps. Catheter 
dislodgement can occur with any CVC and move out of central circulation in which case the 
catheter should be replaced. Pinch-off syndrome refers to the compression of the subclavian vein
